name: Betaine
lead: Betaine, also called trimethylglycine (TMG) or glycine betaine, is a small N-trimethylated amino acid derivative first isolated from sugar beets, after which it is named [1][2]. It occurs in beets, spinach, quinoa, wheat and seafood, is made in the body from choline, and acts both as a methyl donor in one-carbon metabolism and as an osmolyte that protects cells under stress [1][2].

As a sports supplement, betaine anhydrous is taken by lifters in the hope of improving strength, power and body composition; it appears in pre-workout powders and is marketed with claims about cell hydration, cortisol and recovery [11][12][13].

Human trials on exercise performance are small and short, with some reporting benefits and others reporting none [4][5][6]. A separate pharmaceutical betaine is prescribed for homocystinuria [2]. The term 'betaine' also covers a chemical class, and betaine hydrochloride sold for digestion is a different product [1].

paras: Betaine anhydrous is taken for strength and power training and sometimes for body composition. T Nation's pre-workout products list 2 to 2.5 g servings alongside citrulline malate and beta-alanine [11][12][13][14]. The site's descriptions say betaine promotes intracellular hydration and cell volumisation and reduces cortisol to mitigate overtraining stress [13][15]. Forum users list it among pre-workout ingredients in training logs [16].

Betaine is a prescription medicine for homocystinuria, a genetic disorder of methionine metabolism, according to Grokipedia [2]. A registered trial studied betaine metabolism in homocystinuria (NCT02404337) [20]. Other trials have examined betaine in peroxisome biogenesis disorders, steatohepatitis, lipid metabolism in overweight women and in lactating mothers [21][22][23][24][25]. Cosmetic products use betaine as a humectant and skin conditioner, and cocamidopropyl betaine derivatives are surfactants in shampoos [1][2].

A 2010 review in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition discussed ergogenic effects of betaine on strength and power [3]. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis examined chronic betaine supplementation and exercise performance [4]. A 2020 trial reported that betaine did not improve muscle hypertrophy or strength after six weeks of CrossFit training [5]. A 2025 randomised trial in cyclists reported that betaine improved 60 km time-trial performance and one-carbon metabolism during recovery [6]. Registered trials include betaine with blood flow restriction training (NCT05790070), exercise and gut permeability (NCT06392360) and firefighter thermoregulation (NCT06042270) [26][27][28].

Grokipedia reports low toxicity, a generally recognised as safe classification for food use, and rapid absorption with peak plasma levels within about an hour [2]. An observational literature links gut-microbe metabolism of choline-containing compounds to trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO) and cardiovascular risk [8][9]; a trial examined TMAO in vegetarians [10]. These studies concern choline pathways and are not direct tests of betaine supplements.

Betaine donates a methyl group to convert homocysteine to methionine through betaine-homocysteine S-methyltransferase, and is an osmoprotectant that stabilises proteins and cell structures under osmotic stress [2][29]. Proposed performance mechanisms include cell hydration, support for creatine synthesis and anabolic signalling; the sources cited do not show these mechanisms in healthy trainees. Betaine has also been studied in inflammation research [30] and in nutrition and epigenetics reviews [32].

Betaine was first isolated in 1869 from sugar beet molasses by Hermann Scheibler, according to Grokipedia, which also dates the elucidation of its methyl-donor role to the 1940s and its osmoprotectant role in bacteria to the 1960s [2]; these dates come from an AI-generated source and were not independently verified. Wikipedia notes that historically the term was reserved for trimethylglycine [1].
Exercise: a 2010 review [3], a 2024 meta-analysis [4], a six-week CrossFit trial [5] and a 2025 cycling trial [6], with registered trials listed above [26][27][28].
Other conditions: registered trials in homocystinuria, peroxisome disorders, steatohepatitis and lipid metabolism [20][21][22][23][25].

lore.intro: Betaine appears on T Nation almost entirely as an ingredient in the site's own pre-workouts and in training logs; discussion of betaine HCl for digestion is a separate topic [11][12][16][17].

claims.believers: Pre-workout marketing and forum users include betaine for strength and cell volumisation [13][16].
claims.experts: A review discussed ergogenic effects [3] and a meta-analysis has examined it [4]; a six-week CrossFit trial reported no hypertrophy or strength improvement [5].

claims.claim: Betaine reduces cortisol and prevents overtraining
claims.believers: A T Nation supplement article describes betaine anhydrous as reducing cortisol to mitigate overtraining stress [15].
claims.experts: No study cited here tests cortisol effects of betaine in trained people.

claims.claim: Betaine promotes cell hydration and volumisation
claims.believers: T Nation's description of a pre-workout says betaine promotes intracellular hydration and cell volumisation [13].
claims.experts: Betaine's osmolyte role is established in cell biology [2][29]; whether this translates to muscle hydration or size in supplement users has not been shown in the sources cited.

claims.claim: Betaine HCl and apple cider vinegar help digestion
claims.believers: One poster said they were about to try betaine HCl with ACV for the fourth or fifth time for a digestive problem [17].
claims.experts: Betaine hydrochloride is a different compound from betaine anhydrous [1]; no study cited here tests it.
